title: Pasta Carbonara
subtitle: A Roman classic of silk-smooth egg and cheese sauce with crispy pancetta
excerpt: Carbonara is one of Rome's great pasta dishes. The trick is keeping the heat low enough so the egg yolks coat the pasta without scrambling. No cream is needed, ever.
sourceNotes: Carbonara originated in Rome, with roots in the mid-20th century. The defining technique is emulsifying egg yolks and Parmesan with pasta water.

recipe.makeAheadNotes: The pancetta can be cooked up to an hour ahead and kept warm.

content.text: The key to carbonara is temperature. Too hot and you get scrambled eggs on pasta. Work quickly off the heat, and the sauce will turn glossy and cling to every strand.
Bring a large pot of heavily salted water to the boil. Cook the spaghetti according to packet instructions until al dente.
While the pasta cooks, put the pancetta and garlic in a cold frying pan. Set over medium heat and cook for 8 to 10 minutes until the pancetta is golden and crisp. Discard the garlic.
Whisk the egg yolks with most of the Parmesan. Season with black pepper.
Reserve a mugful (about 200ml) of pasta water before draining. Drain the spaghetti and add it to the pancetta pan. Take the pan off the heat.
Pour in the egg mixture and toss quickly. Add pasta water, a splash at a time, tossing constantly until you have a silky sauce that coats the pasta.
Divide between bowls. Top with the remaining Parmesan and more black pepper.

items.symptom: The sauce has scrambled into chunks.
items.cause: The pan was too hot when you added the egg mixture.
items.fix: Always take the pan off the heat before adding eggs.

items.symptom: The sauce is too thick and gluey.
items.cause: Not enough pasta water was added.
items.fix: Add more hot pasta water and toss vigorously.

items.symptom: The sauce is watery and won't cling.
items.cause: Too much pasta water was added at once.
items.fix: Let it sit 30 seconds off heat to thicken slightly.
